analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act's annual fee on health insurance companies.
analysis.headline: A bill with 39 Senate cosponsors — all Republicans — to repeal the health insurance industry's annual Affordable Care Act fee died in the Senate Finance Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would erase Section 9010 of the Affordable Care Act, which charges health insurers an annual fee based on their net premium income. Insurers generally pass that fee into the premiums they charge, so sponsors pitched repeal as "protecting patients from higher premiums." The direct, certain winner is the insurance industry, which would stop paying the fee; households would see lower premiums only if insurers passed the savings along, and the federal government would lose billions in annual revenue with nothing to replace it.
analysis.who_benefits: Health insurance companies gain the most: they would stop paying an annual fee calculated on their net premium income [S2][S3]. Consumers and employers with fully insured coverage would benefit only indirectly, and only to the extent insurers pass the savings through as lower premiums — the fee is built into premium prices, so some relief was plausible, but nothing in the bill requires insurers to lower premiums rather than keep the difference.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Health insurance companies; modest premium relief possible

how_it_helps.text: Strikes the ACA provision requiring health insurers to pay an annual fee based on their net premium income, directly eliminating that cost from the industry's books.

The bill's stated rationale (its second section is titled "Protecting Patients from Higher Premiums") is that because insurers build the fee into the premiums they charge, repeal would lower premiums for households and employers with fully insured health plans — by independent estimates, roughly 1–2% of premiums.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government, and ultimately taxpayers: repealing the fee removes billions of dollars in annual revenue, widening deficits over the next decade unless Congress offsets the loss with other cuts or taxes. If insurers do not pass the full savings into premiums, consumers pay the fee in premiums while the industry pockets the relief.

drawbacks.text: Repeal removes billions of dollars in annual federal revenue — roughly $100 billion over ten years by widely cited estimates — with no offset in the bill, adding directly to deficits or requiring equivalent cuts to other programs.

Nothing in the bill guarantees the savings reach consumers. The fee is charged to insurers, but whether repeal shows up as lower premiums or as higher insurer profits depends entirely on market behavior the bill does not regulate.
The fee is general federal revenue that helps pay for the rest of the Affordable Care Act; repealing it without a replacement weakens the financing behind the law's coverage provisions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost side is large and certain — a decade-scale revenue loss to the Treasury, concentrated on a profitable industry. The benefit to ordinary people is real but smaller and conditional: premium relief of only a percent or two, delivered only if insurers choose to pass the savings on. As a consumer-relief measure it is poorly targeted; as an industry tax cut it is direct and unconditional. An honest supporter would acknowledge that pairing repeal with an offset, or conditioning it on premium reductions, would have served consumers far better.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced with 39 cosponsors, the bill was sent to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was filed, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Senator John Barrasso introduced the bill on January 16, 2015, joined on the day of introduction by 21 other Republican senators including Orrin Hatch, the Finance Committee's chair.
In total, 39 Republican senators cosponsored the bill in a Senate where Republicans held the majority.

The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Finance Committee the same day it was introduced; the action history records no hearing, no markup, and no vote — that referral was the bill's last action for the next two years.
The 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 with the bill still parked in committee, so the ACA's insurer fee stayed on the books.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal Treasury kept collecting the insurers' fee, and health insurers kept paying a tax their industry had sponsored legislation to repeal. Consumers saw no change either way: the fee stayed embedded in premiums, and no repeal savings ever arrived.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Treasury; insurers kept paying the fee

for.name: Sen. John Barrasso
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 16, 2015 to repeal the ACA's annual fee on health insurers.

for.name: 39 of 54 Senate Republicans
for.role: Cosponsors, including Finance Chairman Orrin Hatch and 20 other original cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it the backing of a large share of the majority-party caucus.

for.name: America's Health Insurance Plans (AHIP)
for.what_they_did: Lobbied for years for repeal of the ACA health insurer fee, the tax this bill would eliminate.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, Republican-chaired in the 114th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress; notably, the committee's chairman was himself an original cosponsor.

sides.party_line_note: All 39 cosponsors were Republicans in a Republican-run Senate, yet no floor vote ever occurred, so no recorded vote split exists; the bill's failure came from committee inaction rather than an opposing vote.

industries.note: Repeal would permanently remove an annual fee the industry pays on its premium income — a direct, unconditional cost saving worth billions a year. Because insurers pass the fee into premiums, consumers could share modestly in the gain, but nothing in the bill obliges them to, and the Treasury would lose the revenue either way.

industries.industry: Employers and households with fully insured health plans
industries.note: Fully insured plans pay the fee through their premiums; repeal would lower those premiums by a percent or two if insurers pass the savings through. Self-insured employers, who pay the fee indirectly, are less affected.
The fee raises roughly $8 billion a year in general revenue; repealing it without an offset adds to deficits that taxpayers ultimately bear.
